# [LumiLettuce] Descriptive & Inferential Statistics

## I. Load libraries and inspect data set

Load the necessary libraries and create path to tidy data set. Read the tidy data set file in the form of RDS. This is better than .csv version because the RDS can save particular objects. For example, it preserves the variable type of each column making analysis easier.

```{r 00_load}

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)      # to make figures
library(kableExtra)   # to make tables
library(factoextra)   # to make PCA
library(patchwork)
library(car)          # Levene's test
library(vegan)      # For diversity() function
library(ggsignif)
library(rstatix)
library(phyloseq)
library(gt)
library(ggsci)
library(RColorBrewer) # to make figures
library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)

# Use the function 'here' to create a path to tidy data set
data_tidy_path <- here::here("data/processed") 
    #data_tidy_path
    #list.files(data_tidy_path) 

# the RDS file is generated by companion script to tidy data (blueC_data_tidying_R)
lumilettuce <- readRDS(file.path(data_tidy_path,"full_data.rds")) 
    
glimpse(lumilettuce) 
head(lumilettuce)

```

There are 24 columns and 18,988 rows in this data set. It includes both the microbiome data and the metadata. There are categorical and continuous variables.

## II. Abiotic environment

### 1. Abiotic summary table

Many of the metadata variables are continuous environmental parameters. They help us to understand the context. Some, could also be interesting to explore later on to see if there are correlations in the data associated with these continuous variables. This table compares the metrics (mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, minimum, and maximum) for the continuous environmental variables of the data set across all diel phases between the two sites. This helps us establish the baseline environmental conditions across sites and time of day.

```{r 01_summary_table}

table_summary_continuous <- lumilettuce                                     |>
  filter(!is.na(sample_id), !is.na(diel_phase), !is.na(site_name), !is.na(temp_degC), !is.na(salinity_psu), !is.na(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L), !is.na(pH), !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s))                                                    |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                     |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols        = c(temp_degC, dissolved_oxygen_mg_L, pH, salinity_psu,      
           PAR_umol_photons_m2_s),
           names_to = "Variable",
           values_to = "Value")                                             |>
  # Change the name of the Variable column to make it better suited for a table
  mutate(
    Variable    = case_when(
      Variable  == "temp_degC" ~ "Temperature (°C)",
      Variable  == "dissolved_oxygen_mg_L" ~ "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)",
      Variable  == "pH" ~ "pH",
      Variable  == "salinity_psu" ~ "Salinity (PSU)",
      Variable  == "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s" ~ "PAR (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹)",
      TRUE ~ Variable)
    )                                                                       |>
  # There will be a top-header and a sub-header for site name and descriptive   
  # statistic variable, respectively
  group_by(diel_phase, Variable, site_name)                                             |>
  summarise(
    Mean        = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    SD          = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median      = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    IQR         = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Min - Max` = sprintf("%.2f - %.2f", min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), max(Value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups     = "drop")                                                   |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = site_name,
    values_from = c(Mean, SD, Median, IQR, `Min - Max`),
    names_glue  = "{site_name}_{.value}")                                   |>
 arrange(diel_phase, Variable)                                              |>
  select(
    diel_phase, Variable,
    Pescalgarve_Mean, Pescalgarve_SD, Pescalgarve_Median, Pescalgarve_IQR, `Pescalgarve_Min - Max`,
    `Ria de Alvor_Mean`, `Ria de Alvor_SD`, `Ria de Alvor_Median`, `Ria de Alvor_IQR`, `Ria de Alvor_Min - Max`
  )

# This is not the final table
View(table_summary_continuous)

table_summary_continuous                                                    |>
  select(-diel_phase)                                                       |>
  kbl(
    # Sub-headers for metrics
    col.names   = c("Variable", 
                    "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR", "Min - Max", 
                    "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR", "Min - Max"),
    align       = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_classic(
    full_width  = FALSE, 
    html_font   = "Times New Roman",
    font_size   = 13)                                                       |>
  # Top header spanning across site groups
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Pescalgarve" = 5, "Ria de Alvor" = 5))       |>
  pack_rows("Dawn", 1, 5)                                                   |>
  pack_rows("Noon", 6, 10)                                                  |>
  pack_rows("Dusk", 11, 15)                                                 |>
  pack_rows("Midnight", 16, 20)                                             |>
  
  # Save this table as a .png in correct folder in directory to add to manuscript
  save_kable(file = "../output/tables/table_summary_continuous.png", zoom = 3)

```

When comparing between the two sites, we can already see that that the standard variation is 0 at all times for Ria de Alvor, which makes sense because there is a sample size n=1 for all site/diel phase combination. Dissolved oxygen (DO) and pH are quite similar in both sites. The largest differences for sites are pH, salinity, and PAR.

DO, salinity, and pH remain stable across all time points. PAR varies a lot because it remains low at dawn, dusk, and midnight, with the lowest values at dawn, but then has a peak increase at noon. This pattern is consistent across both sites. Temperature appears to fluctuate slightly during the day.

### 2. Boxplots for continuous environmental variables

The continuous environmental variables temperature, PAR, and salinity showed interesting variation in the table. These boxplots explore the abiotic parameters and how they fluctuate in function of site and tiem of day.

```{r 02_boxplot_DO}
# Remove NAs
boxplot_env_data <- lumilettuce                                            |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                    |>
  filter(!is.na(diel_phase), !is.na(site_name), !is.na(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L), !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s), !is.na(salinity_psu), !is.na(temp_degC), !is.na(temp_degC)) |>
  # To remove the water samples
  filter(sample_type != "Water filter" | is.na(sample_type)) 

# Boxplot for DO
boxplot_DO <- ggplot(boxplot_env_data, aes(x = diel_phase,y = dissolved_oxygen_mg_L, fill = site_name, colour = site_name)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha           = 0.2, # opacity
    outlier.shape   = NA, # no need to show outliers
    width           = 0.5,
    position        = position_dodge(width=0.75)
  ) +
  # Add a diamond shape for the mean of each box
  stat_summary(
    aes(group       = site_name),           
    fun             = mean,
    geom            = "point",
    shape           = 23,                       
    size            = 3.5,
    colour          = "black",                 
    fill            = "black",                  
    position        = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position        = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width =0.15, dodge.width=0.75),
    size            = 2.5,
    alpha           = 0.3,
  ) +
  # Teal for Pescalgarve and orchid for Ria de Alvor
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Pescalgarve"="#008080", "Ria de Alvor"="#DA70D6")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("Pescalgarve"="#008080", "Ria de Alvor"="#DA70D6")) +
  theme_classic(base_size =12) +
  labs(
    x               = "Diel Phase",
    y               = "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)",
    fill            = "Site Name",
    colour          = "Site Name"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title      = element_text(face="bold"),
    axis.text       = element_text(colour="black"),
    legend.position = "right",
    lengend.title   = element_text(face="bold")
  )

# Display DO boxplot
boxplot_DO

# Save the DO boxplot
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/boxplot_DO.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)


```

There are 9 observations for each box with 3 unique values for each box of Pescalgarve. A black diamond symbolizing the mean was added to each box. Ria de Alvor only has 9 of the same measurements (repeated) for each diel phase.

Pescalgarve has a slight increase in DO at dusk, whereas the other diel phases appear stable at around 10 mg/L. Ria de Alvor shows a greater increase at noon and dusk before going back down at midnight. Ria de Alvor varies between 9 and 11 mg/L.

### 3. Multifaceted boxplot abiotic variables

This will generate one figure with all the abiotic variable boxplots and only show the legend once to avoid repetitions.

```{r 07_multipanel_environmental_boxplots}

# Filter and clean the data
boxplot_env_data <- lumilettuce                                                 |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                         |>
  filter(
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L),
    !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s),
    !is.na(salinity_psu),
    !is.na(temp_degC),
    !is.na(pH)
  )                                                                             |>
  filter(sample_type != "Water filter" | is.na(sample_type))

# Generate standardized boxplots
create_env_boxplot <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = diel_phase, y = .data[[y_var]], fill = site_name, colour = site_name)) +
    geom_boxplot(
      alpha         = 0.2,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      width         = 0.5,
      position      = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
    ) +
    stat_summary(
      aes(group = site_name),
      fun      = mean,
      geom     = "point",
      shape    = 23,
      size     = 3.5,
      colour   = "black",
      fill     = "black",
      position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
    ) +
    geom_point(
      position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.75),
      size     = 2.5,
      alpha    = 0.3
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      x      = "Diel Phase",
      y      = y_label,
      fill   = "Site Name",
      colour = "Site Name"
    ) +
    theme(
      axis.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text       = element_text(colour = "black"),
      legend.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 25),
      legend.text     = element_text(size = 20),
      # Add a solid border, light background, and padding around the legend box
      legend.box.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9, fill = "grey"),
      legend.margin         = margin(t = 10, r = 12, b = 10, l = 12)
    )
}

# Create the 5 individual subplots
p_do   <- create_env_boxplot(boxplot_env_data, "dissolved_oxygen_mg_L", "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)")
p_par  <- create_env_boxplot(boxplot_env_data, "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s", expression(bold(paste("PAR (", mu, "mol photons m"^-2*" s"^-1*")"))))
p_sal  <- create_env_boxplot(boxplot_env_data, "salinity_psu", "Salinity (PSU)")
p_temp <- create_env_boxplot(boxplot_env_data, "temp_degC", "Temperature (°C)")
p_ph   <- create_env_boxplot(boxplot_env_data, "pH", "pH")

# Assemble with patchwork
# - guide_area() fills the 6th slot with the collected legend
# - tag_levels supplies A-E for the 5 plots and leaves the 6th empty ("")
multi_abiotic_boxplot <- (p_do + p_par + p_sal + p_temp + p_ph + guide_area()) +
  plot_layout(
    ncol   = 3,
    nrow   = 2,
    guides = "collect"
  ) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = list(c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "")),
    theme      = theme(
      plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
    )
  ) &
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside"
  )

print(multi_abiotic_boxplot)

# Save
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/multipanel_environmental_boxplots.png",
  plot     = multi_abiotic_boxplot,
  width    = 13,
  height   = 8.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

### 4. Mann-Whitney U test & Kruskal-Wallis

First, I will verify whether my data is normally distributed for each environmental variable using the Shapiro-Wilk test. The null hypothesis (if the p-value is greater than 0.05) states that the data is normally distributed. Then, I will test for the homogeneity of variances. The null hypothesis states that the variances are equal across all groups. If the data is parametric, i will perform a Two-Way ANOVA. If not, I will perform a Mann-Whitney U Test for site_name (2 levels) and a Kruskall-Wallis for diel_phase (4 levels). I can then perform a Dunn test to see where the significant differences are.

```{r 08_abiotic_test}
# Check for normality using Shapiro-Wilk test
shapiro.test(boxplot_env_data$dissolved_oxygen_mg_L) # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(boxplot_env_data$PAR_umol_photons_m2_s) # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(boxplot_env_data$salinity_psu)          # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(boxplot_env_data$temp_degC)             # data is not normally distributed
shapiro.test(boxplot_env_data$pH)                    # data is not normally distributed

# Create boxplots for both variables to see whether there are outliers
boxplot(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data) # outliers
boxplot(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data)  # no outliers

boxplot(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data) # outliers
boxplot(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data)  # outliers

boxplot(salinity_psu ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data) # outliers
boxplot(salinity_psu ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data)  #  no outliers

boxplot(temp_degC ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data) # outliers
boxplot(temp_degC ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data)  #  no outliers

boxplot(pH ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data) # outliers
boxplot(pH ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data)  #  no outliers

# Perform Levene's test for homogeneity of variances
# Use center = median if there are outliers (more robust)

leveneTest(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, center = median) # not equal
leveneTest(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, center = mean)  # not equal

leveneTest(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, center = median) # not equal
leveneTest(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, center = median) # equal

leveneTest(salinity_psu ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, center = median) # equal
leveneTest(salinity_psu ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, center = mean) # not equal

leveneTest(temp_degC ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, center = median) # not equal
leveneTest(temp_degC ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, center = mean) # not equal

leveneTest(pH ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, center = median) # equal
leveneTest(pH ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, center = mean) # not equal

# Mann-Whitney U test for site_nmae
wilcox.test(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, exact = FALSE) # significant diff
wilcox.test(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, exact = FALSE) # no diff
wilcox.test(salinity_psu ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, exact = FALSE)          # significant diff
wilcox.test(temp_degC ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, exact = FALSE)             # significant diff
wilcox.test(pH ~ site_name, data = boxplot_env_data, exact = FALSE)                    # significant diff

# Kruskal-Wallis test for diel_phase
kruskal.test(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data)              # significant diff
kruskal.test(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data)              # significant diff
kruskal.test(salinity_psu ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data)                       # no diff
kruskal.test(temp_degC ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data)                          # no diff   
kruskal.test(pH ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data)                                 # significant diff

# Dunn test for significantly different variables
dunn_test(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, p.adjust.method = "holm") # dawn and dusk
dunn_test(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, p.adjust.method = "holm")
dunn_test(pH ~ diel_phase, data = boxplot_env_data, p.adjust.method = "holm")

```

All the p-values for the Shapiro-Wilk test are smaller than 0.05, which means that I must reject the null hypothesis. This means that the data is not normally distributed. The homogeneity of variances also fails in most cases, meaning the data is non-parametric. The Mann-Whitney U test showed significant difference between both sites for all variables except PAR.

The Kruskal-Wallis test showed significant difference between diel phases for DO, PAR, and pH.

The Dunn test shows that the significant difference for DO is between dawn and dusk, which is consistent with the previous box plot. For PAR, the largest significant differences are between dawn and noon and noon and midnight, then between dusk and midnight, and finally between noon and dusk. For pH, the largest significant difference is between noon and midnight, then dawn and noon, and finally noon and dusk.

### 5. PCA abiotic variables

This Principle component analysis (PCA) looks at the five (5) abiotic variables and the two sites. The direction and length of the arrows indicates how strongly each variable correlates with the axes and with each other.

```{r 09_pca_abiotic}

# Define environmental variables
env_vars <- c("dissolved_oxygen_mg_L", "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s", 
              "salinity_psu", "temp_degC", "pH")

# Filter complete cases
pca_data <- boxplot_env_data |>
  drop_na(all_of(env_vars), site_name)

# Perform PCA (center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE is essential for mixed units)
pca_env <- prcomp(pca_data[, env_vars], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

# Clean variable labels for vector arrows
pretty_labels <- c(
  "dissolved_oxygen_mg_L" = "DO",
  "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s" = "PAR",
  "salinity_psu"          = "Salinity",
  "temp_degC"             = "Temp",
  "pH"                    = "pH"
)
rownames(pca_env$rotation) <- pretty_labels[rownames(pca_env$rotation)]

# Generate the PCA Biplot
pca_abiotic <- fviz_pca_biplot(
  pca_env,
  title           = NULL,
  geom.ind        = "point",
  habillage       = pca_data$site_name,
  palette         = c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6"),
  pointshape      = 19,
  pointsize       = 3,
  alpha.ind       = 0.7,
  addEllipses     = TRUE,               # 95% concentration ellipses
  ellipse.type    = "convex",           # "convex" polygon or "confidence" ellipse
  ellipse.alpha   = 0.15,
  col.var         = "black",            # Vector arrow styling
  arrowsize       = 0.7,
  repel           = TRUE,               # Avoid text label overlap
  labelsize       = 4.5
) +
  labs(
    color    = "Site Name",
    fill     = "Site Name",
    shape    = "Site Name"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text       = element_text(colour = "black"),
    legend.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.box.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6, fill = "grey98"),
    legend.margin   = margin(8, 10, 8, 10)
  )

print(pca_abiotic)

# Save
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/pca_abiotic.png",
  plot     = pca_abiotic,
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 6.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

The first two principle components account for 67.3% of the total variance, which is adequate. The primary drivers of Dim1 (39.2%) are dissolved oxygen and pH. The primary drivers of Dim2 (28.1%) are temperature and salinity, with PAR also playing a smaller role. The samples from Pescalgarve clustered almost exclusively in the negative values of Dim2 which means that suggests that they are characterized by lower temperature and salinity. Ria de Alvor samples are fewer and clustered in the positive values of Dim2, characterized by higher temperatures and salinities. Pescalgarve samples also span across a wide range of Dim1 and Dim2 suggesting greater environmental variability than the tighter cluster of Ria de Alvor. This suggests Ria de Alvor has a more stable and homogeneous environment than Pescalgarve.

## III. Host vs. water specificity

### 1. Taxonomic stacked barplot *Ulva* and seawater

This is a broad taxonomic stacked barplot for the relative abundance between Ulva and seawater across sites. The bacteria are shown at the order level. This allows us to have a quick overview of which bacterial orders are found in both water filter samples and the seaweed, and which are unique to the seaweed host.

```{r 10_barplot_ulva_seawater}

# Filter data for valid sites, and sample types (Ulva vs Seawater)
bacteria_data <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(!is.na(order), order != "", order != "unknown", order != "Unclassified") |>
  filter(sample_type %in% c("Ulva", "Water filter"), !is.na(site_name)) 


# Identify the Top 10 most abundant bacterial Orders across the data set
top_10_orders <- bacteria_data |>
  group_by(order) |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(order_by = total_count, n = 10) |>
  pull(order)

# Collapse lower-abundance orders into "Other" and calculate Relative Abundance (%)
order_rel_abund <- bacteria_data |>
  mutate(
    order_grouped = if_else(order %in% top_10_orders, order, "Other (< 2%)")
  ) |>
  # Aggregate counts per Site, Sample Type, and Order
  group_by(site_name, sample_type, order_grouped) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  # Convert to relative abundance percentage (sums to 100% per bar)
  mutate(relative_abundance = (count / sum(count)) * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # Reorder factors so "Other" is at the bottom of the stack and dominant orders are on top
  mutate(
    order_grouped = factor(
      order_grouped,
      levels = c("Other (< 2%)", rev(top_10_orders))
    )
  )

# Custom distinct color palette (10 distinct colors and neutral grey for 'Other')
custom_colors <- c(
  "Other (< 2%)"       = "#D3D3D3",
  "Pseudomonadales"    = "#1F77B4",
  "Flavobacteriales"   = "#FF7F0E",
  "Enterobacterales"   = "#2CA02C",
  "Cytophagales"       = "#D62728",
  "Chitinophagales"    = "#9467BD",
  "Bacteroidales"      = "#8C564B",
  "Rhodobacterales"    = "#E377C2",
  "Caulobacterales"    = "#7F7F7F",
  "Sphingobacteriales" = "#BCBD22",
  "Burkholderiales"    = "#17BECF"
)

# Create the stacked barplot
barplot_ulva_seawater <- ggplot(order_rel_abund, aes(x = sample_type, y = relative_abundance, fill = order_grouped)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack", width = 0.65, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~site_name) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors, guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02)), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    x    = "Sample Type",
    y    = "Relative Abundance (%)",
    fill = "Microbial Order"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.title        = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text         = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11),
    strip.text        = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    strip.background  = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = "grey93", linewidth = 0.6),
    legend.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text       = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position   = "right",
    panel.spacing     = unit(1.5, "lines")
  )


print(barplot_ulva_seawater)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/barplot_ulva_seawater.png",
  plot     = barplot_ulva_seawater,
  width    = 9.5,
  height   = 6,
  dpi      = 300
)


```

We can see from this barplot that the two dominant bacterial orders are Pseudomonadales and Flavobacteriales for both sample types at both sites. At Pescalgarve, the Ulva samples contain more Cytophagales than in the water filter sample. This suggests that Ulva recruits this order specifically. The same is seen in the samples collected at Ria de Alvor. In the seaweed sample of Ria de Alvor, we see less Flavobacteriales than in the water filter sample. The Pescalgarve seaweed sample also has more Chitinophagales than in the respective water filter sample.

### 2. Alpha diversity comparison

The alpha diversity analysis helps portray the bacterial community in both sites and in both sample types. Three comparisons are performed here: observed species richness, Shannon's diversity index (H'), and Pielou's evenness (J').

```{r 11_alpha_diversity_ulva_vs_seawater}

# Filter for valid sample types
bact_data <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    sample_type %in% c("Ulva", "Water filter"),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(genus),
    count > 0
  ) 

# Calculate alpha diversity metrics per sample_id
alpha_metrics <- bact_data |>
  group_by(sample_id, sample_type, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  summarise(
    Observed_Richness = n_distinct(genus),
    Shannon = diversity(count, index = "shannon"),
    Evenness = Shannon / log(Observed_Richness),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(alpha_metrics)


# Build standardized alpha diversity box plots

create_alpha_boxplot <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = sample_type, y = .data[[y_var]], fill = sample_type, colour = sample_type)) +
    geom_boxplot(
      alpha         = 0.3,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      width         = 0.45,
      colour        = "black",
      linewidth     = 0.6
    ) +
    # Add diamond shape for the mean
    stat_summary(
      fun      = mean,
      geom     = "point",
      shape    = 23,
      size     = 3.5,
      colour   = "black",
      fill     = "black"
    ) +
    # Jittered individual sample points
    geom_jitter(
      width = 0.15,
      size  = 2.5,
      alpha = 0.6
    ) +
    # Color scheme: green for Ulva, blue for seawater
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#2E8B57", "Water filter" = "#4682B4")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#2E8B57", "Water filter" = "#4682B4")) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      x      = "Sample Type",
      y      = y_label,
      fill   = "Sample Type",
      colour = "Sample Type"
    ) +
    theme(
      axis.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text       = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11),
      legend.position = "none" 
    )
}


# Generate the 3 individual alpha diversity subplots
p_richness <- create_alpha_boxplot(alpha_metrics, "Observed_Richness", "Observed Genus Richness")
p_shannon  <- create_alpha_boxplot(alpha_metrics, "Shannon", "Shannon Diversity Index (H')")
p_evenness <- create_alpha_boxplot(alpha_metrics, "Evenness", "Pielou's Evenness (J')")


# Faceted box plot comparing Ulva vs seawater across both sites
create_faceted_alpha <- function(data, y_var, y_label) {
  create_alpha_boxplot(data, y_var, y_label) +
    facet_wrap(~site_name) +
    theme(
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      strip.background = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = "grey93", linewidth = 0.5)
    )
}

p_rich_site <- create_faceted_alpha(alpha_metrics, "Observed_Richness", "Observed Genus Richness")
p_shan_site <- create_faceted_alpha(alpha_metrics, "Shannon", "Shannon Diversity Index (H')")
p_even_site <- create_faceted_alpha(alpha_metrics, "Evenness", "Pielou's Evenness (J')")

combined_site_alpha <- (p_rich_site / p_shan_site / p_even_site) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

print(combined_site_alpha)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/alpha_diversity_ulva_vs_seawater.png",
  plot     = combined_site_alpha,
  width    = 8,
  height   = 10,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

The observed genus richness appears to be similar between sample types from Pescalgarve, but not in Ria de Alvor. The Shannon diversity index appears to be the same for both sample types in Pescalgarve again, but a slight difference for the water filter samples at Ria de Alvor. The evenness seems very similar across sample type and site.

### 3. Mann-Whiteny U Test

First, I will verify whether my data is normally distributed for each environmental variable using the Shapiro-Wilk test. The null hypothesis (if the p-value is greater than 0.05) states that the data is normally distributed. Then, I will test for the homogeneity of variances. The null hypothesis states that the variances are equal across all groups. If the data is parametric, i will perform a Two-Way ANOVA. If not, I will perform a Mann-Whitney U Test for site_name (2 levels) and sample type (2 levels).

```{r 12_mann_whitney_alpha}

shapiro.test(alpha_metrics$Observed_Richness) # not normally distributed
shapiro.test(alpha_metrics$Shannon)           # not normally distributed
shapiro.test(alpha_metrics$Evenness)          # not normally distributed

boxplot(Observed_Richness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
boxplot(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers

boxplot(Shannon ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
boxplot(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
               
boxplot(Evenness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
boxplot(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics) # outliers
# They all have outliers, so it is better to use the median as the center (more robust) for Levene's test

leveneTest(Observed_Richness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous
leveneTest(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous

leveneTest(Shannon ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous
leveneTest(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # homogeneous

leveneTest(Evenness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # not homogeneous
leveneTest(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, center = median) # homogeneous
# The data is not parametric, Mann-Whitney U test must be performed

wilcox.test(Observed_Richness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff
wilcox.test(Observed_Richness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Shannon ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff
wilcox.test(Shannon ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

wilcox.test(Evenness ~ site_name, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff
wilcox.test(Evenness ~ sample_type, data = alpha_metrics, exact = FALSE) # no significant diff

               
```

They all have a p-value greater than 0.01. This means there is no significance difference in observed richness, Shannon diversity, or evenness between seaweed and water samples.

### 4. Principal Coordinates analysis

This section investigates the beta diversity ordination of bacterial communities between Ulva and seawater across sites. These plots are based on abundance-weighed Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and incidence-based Jaccard distance.

```{r 13_pcoa_ulva_water}

# Prepare the data
bact_clean <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    superkingdom == "Bacteria",
    sample_type %in% c("Ulva", "Water filter"),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(genus),
    count > 0
  ) 

# Extract sample-level metadata
metadata <- bact_clean |>
  distinct(sample_id, sample_type, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  arrange(sample_id)

comm_matrix <- bact_clean |>
  # Sum duplicate genus counts per sample first
  group_by(sample_id, genus) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  # Pivot into wide format
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = genus,
    values_from = count,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  arrange(sample_id) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Ensure the metadata matches community matrix rows exactly
metadata <- metadata |> filter(sample_id %in% rownames(comm_matrix))

# Compute dissimilarity matrices & PCoA ordinations

# Bray-Curtis (abundance-weighted)
dist_bc <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "bray")
pcoa_bc <- cmdscale(dist_bc, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

var_bc_1 <- round((pcoa_bc$eig[1] / sum(pcoa_bc$eig[pcoa_bc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)
var_bc_2 <- round((pcoa_bc$eig[2] / sum(pcoa_bc$eig[pcoa_bc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)

df_pcoa_bc <- as.data.frame(pcoa_bc$points) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  rename(PCoA1 = V1, PCoA2 = V2) |>
  left_join(metadata, by = "sample_id")

# Jaccard (presence-absence / incidence-based)
dist_jacc <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
pcoa_jacc <- cmdscale(dist_jacc, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

var_jacc_1 <- round((pcoa_jacc$eig[1] / sum(pcoa_jacc$eig[pcoa_jacc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)
var_jacc_2 <- round((pcoa_jacc$eig[2] / sum(pcoa_jacc$eig[pcoa_jacc$eig > 0])) * 100, 1)

df_pcoa_jacc <- as.data.frame(pcoa_jacc$points) |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  rename(PCoA1 = V1, PCoA2 = V2) |>
  left_join(metadata, by = "sample_id")

# Helper function to plot PCoA ordinations
plot_pcoa <- function(df, var1, var2, dist_name) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = sample_type, fill = sample_type, shape = site_name)) +
    # 95% Normal Confidence Ellipses around Sample Types
    stat_ellipse(
      aes(group = sample_type),
      geom  = "polygon",
      alpha = 0.15,
      type  = "t",
      level = 0.95,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_point(size = 3.5, alpha = 0.85, stroke = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#006400", "Water filter" = "#008ECC")) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Ulva" = "#006400", "Water filter" = "#008ECC")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = 16, "Ria de Alvor" = 17)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      title  = paste("PCoA -", dist_name),
      x      = paste0("PCoA1 (", var1, "%)"),
      y      = paste0("PCoA2 (", var2, "%)"),
      colour = "Sample Type",
      fill   = "Sample Type",
      shape  = "Site Name"
    ) +
    theme(
      plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text       = element_text(colour = "black"),
      legend.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "right",
      legend.box.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5, fill = "grey98"),
      legend.margin   = margin(6, 8, 6, 8)
    )
}

# Generate individual PCoA plots
p_bc   <- plot_pcoa(df_pcoa_bc, var_bc_1, var_bc_2, "Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity")
p_jacc <- plot_pcoa(df_pcoa_jacc, var_jacc_1, var_jacc_2, "Jaccard Distance (Presence-Absence)")

# Combine multi-panel figure & save
combined_pcoa <- (p_bc + p_jacc) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "A",
    theme = theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")


print(combined_pcoa)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/beta_diversity_pcoa_ulva_vs_seawater.png",
  plot     = combined_pcoa,
  width    = 12,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

Thre is a lot of overlap in both plots. This suggests that the surrounding planktonic bacteria share core taxonomic members with the algal surface. The principal coordinates explain a low percentage of total community variance.

### 5. PERMANOVA

This PERMANOVA tests whether community composition varied by sampling site and sample type between the water filter and seaweed samples.

```{r 14_permanova}

bact_clean <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    superkingdom == "Bacteria",
    sample_type %in% c("Ulva", "Water filter"),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  ) 

metadata <- bact_clean |>
  distinct(sample_id, sample_type, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  arrange(sample_id)

# Create the community matrix with id_cols = sample_id
comm_matrix <- bact_clean |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = sample_id,
    names_from  = genus,
    values_from = count,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  arrange(sample_id) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
  as.matrix() 

# Check that it is purely numeric
is.numeric(comm_matrix) # returns TRUE

# Abundance-weighted Bray-Curtis
dist_bray <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "bray")

# Incidence-based Jaccard
dist_jacc <- vegdist(comm_matrix, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)


cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: BRAY-CURTIS ===================\n")
permanova_bray <- adonis2(
  dist_bray ~ sample_type * site_name,
  data         = metadata,
  permutations = 999,
  by           = "margin"
)
print(permanova_bray)

cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: JACCARD ===================\n")
permanova_jacc <- adonis2(
  dist_jacc ~ sample_type * site_name,
  data         = metadata,
  permutations = 999,
  by           = "margin"
)
print(permanova_jacc)


# Test homogeneity of multivariate dispersion (betadisper)
# Tests if within-group variance differs (helps validate PERMANOVA results)

cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Sample Type (Bray-Curtis) ---\n")
disp_type <- betadisper(dist_bray, metadata$sample_type)
print(anova(disp_type))

cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Site Name (Bray-Curtis) ---\n")
disp_site <- betadisper(dist_bray, metadata$site_name)
print(anova(disp_site))

# Visualize dispersions
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(disp_type, main = "Dispersion: Sample Type")
plot(disp_site, main = "Dispersion: Site Name")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

This means that the community composition varied significantly by sampling site and sample type.

## IV. Diel & spatial dynamics of Ulva microbiome

### 1. Order stacked barplots by site and diel phase

This barplot is looking at the relative abundance (%) of orders for each diel phase in both environments. It shows only the 10 dominant orders and the rest is categorized as "Other".

```{r 15_barplot_order_diel}

ulva_clean <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    !is.na(site_name), 
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    sample_type == "Ulva" | (sample_type != "Water filter" & !str_ends(sample_id, regex("w", ignore_case = TRUE))),
    sample_id != "CM"
  ) |>
  mutate(order = replace_na(as.character(order), "Unassigned"))

# Identify the top 10 bacterial orders across all samples
top_10_orders <- ulva_clean |>
  group_by(order) |>
  summarise(total = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(order != "Unassigned") |>
  slice_max(order_by = total, n = 10) |>
  pull(order)

order_data_diel <- ulva_clean |>
  mutate(order_top = if_else(order %in% top_10_orders, order, "Other")) |>
  # Sum counts per sample and order
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, order_top) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  # Compute relative abundance (%) per sample
  mutate(rel_abund = (count / sum(count)) * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # Fill in zeros for unobserved orders per sample while preserving site and phase
  complete(
    nesting(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase),
    order_top,
    fill = list(count = 0, rel_abund = 0)
  ) |>
  # Compute the mean relative abundance across replicates for each site and diel phase
  group_by(site_name, diel_phase, order_top) |>
  summarise(mean_rel_abund = mean(rel_abund, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  # Re-normalize to ensure 100% stack per diel phase
  mutate(mean_rel_abund = (mean_rel_abund / sum(mean_rel_abund)) * 100) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    diel_phase = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Midnight", "Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk")),
    order_top  = factor(order_top, levels = c(top_10_orders, "Other")),
    order_top  = fct_relevel(order_top, "Other", after = Inf)
  )

head(order_data_diel)

# Create the plot with ggplot2
ggplot(order_data_diel, aes(x = diel_phase, y = mean_rel_abund, fill = order_top))         +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2, width = 0.8)              +
  facet_wrap(~ site_name)                                                                  +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100.1), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25))     +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette       = "Paired")                                              + 
  theme_minimal(base_size         = 12)                                                    +
  labs(
    y                             = "Mean Relative Abundance (%)", 
    x                             = "Diel Phase", 
    fill                          = "Order"
  )                                                                                        +
  theme(
    axis.title                    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text                     = element_text(color = "black"),
    strip.text                    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position               = "right",
    legend.title                  = element_text(face = "bold")
  )


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/barplot_order_diel.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)

```

From this, we can see that *Pseudomonadales* is the dominant order in Ria de Alvor at all diel phases. In Pescalgarve, *Flavobacteriales*, *Cytophagales*, and *Pseudomonadales* share the dominance at all diel phases. The mean relative abundance of each order appears to be relatively stable across all diel phases in both environments, with the exception of the order *Bacillales*. This order of bacteria is found in low levels at dawn, noon, and dusk, but they have a peak at midnight. Midnight is the time point of nocturnal respiration. This group is possibly recruited for their function in this metabolic process.

### 2. Heatmap of relative abundance patterns

This heatmap displays the relative abundance patterns of the top 30 bacterial genera associated with the *Ulva* epibiome across four diel phases (Dawn, Noon, Dusk, and Midnight) and both sites. The abundances are standardized across rows using the Z-score. A dark red box signifies strong relative enrichment abundance of the genus (Z ≥ +2) , white is the mean baseline abundance (Z ≈ 0), and dark blue is a strong relative depletion (Z ≤ -2). The genera are grouped by hierarchical clustering based on similar spatial and temporal abundance profiles over a 24-hour cycle.

```{r 16_heatmap_diel}

# Filter Ulva samples 
ulva_clean <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    superkingdom == "Bacteria",
    sample_type == "Ulva",
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  ) |>
  # Sum duplicate entries per genus within each sample
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, genus) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Identify the top 30 most abundant genera on Ulva
top_genera <- ulva_clean |>
  group_by(genus) |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(order_by = total_count, n = 30) |>
  pull(genus)

# Calculate the mean relative abundance (%) per site and diel Phase
ulva_rel <- ulva_clean |>
  filter(genus %in% top_genera) |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  mutate(rel_abund = (count / sum(count)) * 100) |>
  ungroup()

# Average across biological replicates for each condition
heat_df <- ulva_rel |>
  group_by(genus, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  summarise(mean_rel = mean(rel_abund, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  complete(genus, site_name, diel_phase, fill = list(mean_rel = 0))

# Construct matrix & calculate row-wise Z-scores

heat_wide <- heat_df |>
  mutate(
    col_id = paste(site_name, diel_phase, sep = "__")
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = genus,
    names_from  = col_id,
    values_from = mean_rel
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames("genus") |>
  as.matrix()

# Reorder columns chronologically per site
ordered_cols <- c(
  paste("Pescalgarve", c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight"), sep = "__"),
  paste("Ria de Alvor", c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight"), sep = "__")
)
heat_wide <- heat_wide[, ordered_cols]

z_matrix <- t(scale(t(heat_wide)))

z_matrix[is.nan(z_matrix)] <- 0


col_meta <- tibble(col_id = colnames(z_matrix)) |>
  separate(col_id, into = c("Site", "Diel_Phase"), sep = "__")

# Define categorical palette
site_colors <- c("Pescalgarve" = "#008080", "Ria de Alvor" = "#DA70D6")
diel_colors <- c(
  "Midnight" = "#2C3E50", # Dark navy
  "Dawn"     = "#E67E22", # Orange sunrise
  "Noon"     = "#F1C40F", # Bright yellow
  "Dusk"     = "#9B59B6"  # Purple dusk
)

top_anno <- HeatmapAnnotation(
  `Site Name`  = col_meta$Site,
  `Diel Phase` = factor(col_meta$Diel_Phase, levels = c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight")),
  col = list(
    `Site Name`  = site_colors,
    `Diel Phase` = diel_colors
  ),
  annotation_name_side = "left",
  annotation_legend_param = list(
    `Site Name`  = list(title = "Site Name", title_gp = gpar(fontface = "bold")),
    `Diel Phase` = list(title = "Diel Phase", title_gp = gpar(fontface = "bold"))
  )
)

# Diverging color gradient for Z-scores (Blue -> White -> Red)
col_fun <- colorRamp2(c(-2, 0, 2), c("#2166AC", "#F7F7F7", "#B2182B"))

# Plot
ht <- Heatmap(
  z_matrix,
  name               = "Row Z-score",
  col                = col_fun,
  top_annotation     = top_anno,
  column_split       = col_meta$Site, # Visual vertical split between the two sites
  cluster_columns    = FALSE,         # Keep chronological 24-hour cycle intact
  cluster_rows       = TRUE,          # Cluster genera by temporal/spatial co-occurrence
  clustering_distance_rows = "euclidean",
  clustering_method_rows   = "complete",
  show_column_names  = TRUE,
  column_labels      = col_meta$Diel_Phase,
  column_names_rot   = 45,
  column_names_gp    = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"),
  row_names_gp       = gpar(fontsize = 9, fontitalic = TRUE),
  rect_gp            = gpar(col = "white", lwd = 0.5), # Grid border between cells
  heatmap_legend_param = list(
    title_gp         = gpar(fontface = "bold"),
    legend_height    = unit(4, "cm")
  )
)


dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
png("../output/figures/ulva_heatmap_spatial_diel.png", width = 9.5, height = 11, units = "in", res = 300)
draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right", annotation_legend_side = "right")
dev.off()

draw(ht)

```

The enriched genera in Pescalgarve are in the lower half of the heatmap, whereas they are in the upper half of the heatmap for Ria de Alvor.

Bacillus shows high relative enrichment at midnight in both sites, and drops sharply during daytime. There is a dawn bloom at Ria de Alvor at dawn composed of : Pseudoalteromonas, Vibrio, and Alteromonas. The genera Glaciecola, Marinagarivorans, and Acinetobacter spike at noon in Ria de Alvor, whereas they decrease at that same timepoint in Pescalgarve. At dusk, Rhodobacteraceae surges at Pescalgarve along with Hyphomonadaceae_uncultured and Escherichia-Shigella at Ria de Alvor.

### 3. PERMANOVA

This PERMANOVA uses the adonis2 function from the vegan package to evaluate whether whole bacterial community composition changes across sampling site and diel phases. This is a two-way model which can look at the two factors, site name and diel phase, and their interaction.

To avoid false positives caused by unequal dispersion, the assumption of homogeniety of multivariate dispersion must be met. The p-value must be greater than 0.05.

If the interaction term is non-significant, the interaction term will be dropped and an additive model will be run to obtain the exact values for the main effects, as is best practice in statistical analysis.

```{r 17_permanova_community}

ulva_clean <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    superkingdom == "Bacteria",
    sample_type  == "Ulva",
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(diel_phase),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  )

# Extract matching metadata
metadata_ulva <- ulva_clean |>
  distinct(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  mutate(
    diel_phase = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight")),
    site_name  = factor(site_name, levels = c("Pescalgarve", "Ria de Alvor"))
  ) |>
  arrange(sample_id)

# Pivot into a strictly numeric community matrix (Samples x Genera)
comm_matrix_ulva <- ulva_clean |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = sample_id,
    names_from  = genus,
    values_from = count,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  arrange(sample_id) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
  as.matrix()

# Verify alignment
stopifnot(identical(rownames(comm_matrix_ulva), metadata_ulva$sample_id))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Compute dissimilarity matrices
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A. Bray-Curtis (abundance-weighted)
dist_bc <- vegdist(comm_matrix_ulva, method = "bray")

# B. Jaccard (incidence / presence-absence)
dist_jacc <- vegdist(comm_matrix_ulva, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two-way factorial PERMANOVA (adonis2)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# by = "margin" tests marginal (Type III) effects so factor order does not bias results

cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: BRAY-CURTIS ===================\n")
permanova_bc <- adonis2(
  dist_bc ~ site_name * diel_phase,
  data         = metadata_ulva,
  permutations = 999,
  by           = "margin"
)
print(permanova_bc)

cat("\n=================== PERMANOVA: JACCARD ===================\n")
permanova_jacc <- adonis2(
  dist_jacc ~ site_name * diel_phase,
  data         = metadata_ulva,
  permutations = 999,
  by           = "margin"
)
print(permanova_jacc)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Multivariate dispersion (betadisper)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Validate whether site differences are driven by centroid shifts or dispersion
disp_site <- betadisper(dist_bc, metadata_ulva$site_name)
cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Site Name ---\n")
print(anova(disp_site))

disp_diel <- betadisper(dist_bc, metadata_ulva$diel_phase)
cat("\n--- Dispersion Test: Diel Phase ---\n")
print(anova(disp_diel))

# Additive model to test main effects of site and diel phase
fit_bc <- adonis2(dist_bc ~ site_name + diel_phase, data = metadata_ulva, permutations = 999, by = "margin")
fit_jacc <- adonis2(dist_jacc ~ site_name + diel_phase, data = metadata_ulva, permutations = 999, by = "margin")

# Create table 
tidy_adonis <- function(mod, metric_name) {
  as_tibble(mod, rownames = "Factor") |>
    mutate(
      Metric = metric_name,
      Factor = dplyr::recode(Factor,
        "site_name"  = "Site Name",
        "diel_phase" = "Diel Phase",
        "Residual"   = "Residuals",
        "Total"      = "Total"
      )
    ) |>
    rename(
      Df         = Df,
      SumOfSqs   = SumOfSqs,
      R2         = R2,
      F_stat     = F,
      p_val      = `Pr(>F)`
    ) |>
    relocate(Metric, Factor)
}

# 3. Combine both metrics
permanova_table_df <- bind_rows(
  tidy_adonis(fit_bc, "Bray-Curtis"),
  tidy_adonis(fit_jacc, "Jaccard")
)

# 4. Format with `gt`
permanova_gt <- permanova_table_df |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Metric")  |>
  cols_label(
    Factor   = md("**Source of Variation**"),
    Df       = md("**Df**"),
    SumOfSqs = md("**Sum of Squares**"),
    R2       = md("**R²**"),
    F_stat   = md("**Pseudo-F**"),
    p_val    = md("**p-value**")
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = SumOfSqs, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = R2, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = F_stat, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = p_val, decimals = 3) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—") |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.names = "Arial",
    table.font.size = px(13),
    heading.align = "left",
    row_group.font.weight = "bold"
  )

# Display in RStudio Viewer
permanova_gt

gtsave(permanova_gt, "../output/tables/Table_X_PERMANOVA.png")
```

There is no interaction between site name and diel phase according to both distance metrics (Bray-Curtis: F3,64 = 0.68, R2 = 0.026, p-value = 0.916; Jaccard: F3,64 = 0.87, R2 = 0.035, p-value = 0.753). This suggests that the diel changes of the microbiome do not significantly diverge between sites. In other words, The diurnal temporal patterns are not significantly different in the aquaculture facility compared to the natural coastal lagoon.

For the homogeneity of multivariate dispersion, the assumption is met for both variables (site name and diel phase) which confirms that the PERMANOVA tests are robust and unbiased.

The additive model reveals sampling site to be a significant driver of the Ulva microbiome. Indeed, the epibiome differs both in abundance-weighted composition (Bray-Curtis) and membership/turnover (Jaccard). The effect size is larger in Bray-Curtis than in Jaccard (R2: 11.62% \> 8.13%), indicating that site differentiation is primarily driven by shifts in the relative abundances of shared core bacterial genera as well as some taxon replacement. As for diel phase, the model shows whole-community diel stability. Over a 24-hour cycle, the baseline composition remains resilient and stable (p-values \> 0.5).

### 4. Differential abundance analysis

The differential abundance analysis will revela which bacterial genera are significantly enriched during the daytime light peak (Noon) versus the nocturnal phase (Midnight). The method used is the ANCOM-BC2 because it is the gold standard for compositional sequencing count data and adjusts for sampling depth while accounting for covariates (site name). Basically, this method acccounts for sampling fraction differences, handles zero inflation, and includes site name as a covariate.

```{r}
# If not installed:
# BiocManager::install("ANCOMBC")
library(tidyverse)
library(ANCOMBC)
library(mia)
library(SingleCellExperiment)

diel_comp_clean <- lumilettuce |>
  filter(
    superkingdom == "Bacteria",
    sample_type  == "Ulva",
    diel_phase %in% c("Midnight", "Noon"),
    !is.na(site_name),
    !is.na(genus),
    !genus %in% c("Unknown", "Unclassified", ""),
    count > 0
  ) |>
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, genus) |>
  summarise(count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Build count matrix (Genera x Samples)
count_mat <- diel_comp_clean |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = genus,
    names_from  = sample_id,
    values_from = count,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames("genus") |>
  as.matrix()

# Build matching metadata
sample_meta <- diel_comp_clean |>
  distinct(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  mutate(
    # Set Midnight as reference: positive logFC means enriched at Noon
    diel_phase = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Midnight", "Noon")),
    site_name  = factor(site_name, levels = c("Pescalgarve", "Ria de Alvor"))
  ) |>
  arrange(match(sample_id, colnames(count_mat))) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Create TreeSummarizedExperiment / SingleCellExperiment container
tse <- TreeSummarizedExperiment(
  assays  = list(counts = count_mat),
  colData = DataFrame(sample_meta)
)


# Run ANCOM-BC2 model (controlling for site_name)

ancom_res <- ancombc2(
  data         = tse,
  assay_name   = "counts",
  tax_level    = NULL,
  fix_formula  = "site_name + diel_phase",
  p_adj_method = "BH",
  prv_cut      = 0.10, # Keep taxa present in >= 10% of samples
  group        = "diel_phase",
  struc_zero   = TRUE,
  neg_lb       = TRUE
)

# 3. Extract Differentially Abundant Taxa
res_df <- ancom_res$res |>
  select(
    taxon,
    lfc_Noon     = lfc_diel_phaseNoon,
    se_Noon      = se_diel_phaseNoon,
    W_Noon       = W_diel_phaseNoon,
    p_val_Noon   = p_val_diel_phaseNoon,
    q_val_Noon   = q_val_diel_phaseNoon,
    diff_Noon    = diff_diel_phaseNoon
  ) |>
  arrange(q_val_Noon)

# Filter significant taxa (FDR < 0.05)
sig_genera <- res_df |>
  filter(q_val_Noon < 0.05) |>
  mutate(Enrichment = if_else(lfc_Noon > 0, "Noon (Light Peak)", "Midnight (Dark)"))

head(sig_genera, 15)
```

    plot.title   = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

```{r 05_pcoa_loc, eval = FALSE}
# 1. Clean and Prepare
df <- microbiome |> 
  filter(sample_type == "Ulva", site_name != "Unknown") |>
  # Crucial: Convert metadata to factors here so the plot legend is ordered correctly
  mutate(
    diel_phase = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight")),
    site_name = as.factor(site_name)
  )

# A. OTU Table (Counts)
otu_mat <- df |>
  select(sample_id, genus, count) |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus) |> 
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |> # Ensure no duplicate genus/sample rows
  pivot_wider(names_from = genus, values_from = count, values_fill = 0) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
  as.matrix()

# B. Tax Table (Classification)
tax_mat <- df |>
  select(superkingdom, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus) |>
  distinct(genus, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  column_to_rownames("genus") |>
  as.matrix()

# C. Sample Data (Metadata) - MUST be wrapped in sample_data()
# We ensure the row names match the otu_mat row names exactly
s_data <- df |>
  select(sample_id, site_name, morphotype, diel_phase) |>
  distinct() |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# D. Build the Phyloseq Object
# We explicitly convert components to phyloseq classes
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(otu_mat, taxa_are_rows = FALSE), 
  sample_data(s_data), 
  tax_table(tax_mat)
)

# --- VERIFICATION ---
# Run this to make sure 'site_name' is actually inside the object:
sample_variables(ps) 

# --- PLOTTING ---
# 2. Run Ordination
ps_pcoa <- ordinate(ps, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# 3. Plot (Notice the quotes around "site_name")
plot_ordination(ps, ps_pcoa, color = "site_name", shape = "diel_phase") +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = site_name), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#005f73", "Ria do Alvor" = "orange")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#005f73", "Ria do Alvor" = "orange")) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = 24, # Triangle Up
    "Noon"     = 21, # Circle
    "Dusk"     = 25, # Triangle Down
    "Midnight" = 8   # Star
  )) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    color = "Sampling Site",   # Renames the color legend
    shape = "Time of Day",     # Renames the shape legend
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold") # Makes legend titles stand out
  )

     
```

```{r 06_pcoa_pescalgarve, eval = FALSE}
# 1. Subset the phyloseq object to only include Pescalgarve
ps_pesc <- subset_samples(ps, site_name == "Pescalgarve")

# 2. Re-run the ordination
ps_pcoa_pesc <- ordinate(ps_pesc, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# 3. Plot with matching Ellipses and a MERGED legend
plot_ordination(ps_pesc, ps_pcoa_pesc, color = "diel_phase") +
  # Map color, shape, and fill to the same variable
  geom_point(aes(shape = diel_phase, fill = diel_phase), size = 6, alpha = 0.9) +
  
  # Ellipses (show.legend = FALSE keeps the shaded area out of the tiny legend icons)
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = diel_phase), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  # 1. Shape Scale (The Name "Time of Day" must match exactly in all three)
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = 24, # Triangle Up
    "Noon"     = 21, # Circle
    "Dusk"     = 25, # Triangle Down
    "Midnight" = 8   # Star
  )) +
  
  # 2. Color Scale
  scale_color_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = "#C8A2C8", # Lilac
    "Noon"     = "#BDB76B", # Khaki
    "Dusk"     = "#800020", # Burgundy
    "Midnight" = "#2E2E2E"  # Dark Grey
  )) +
  
  # 3. Fill Scale
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = "#C8A2C8", 
    "Noon"     = "#BDB76B", 
    "Dusk"     = "#800020", 
    "Midnight" = "#2E2E2E"
  )) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Axis 1",
    y = "Axis 2"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right" # You can change this to "bottom" if you want more width
  )
```

```{r 08_pcoa_morphotype, eval = FALSE}

# 1. Prepare Metadata (Ensuring 'morphotype' is included this time)
s_data <- df |>
  select(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, morphotype) |> 
  distinct() |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# 2. Rebuild the Phyloseq Object
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(otu_mat, taxa_are_rows = FALSE), 
  sample_data(s_data), 
  tax_table(tax_mat)
)

# 3. Run Ordination (Default is Axis 1 and 2)
ps_pcoa <- ordinate(ps, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# 4. Create the Plot
plot_ordination(ps, ps_pcoa, color = "morphotype", shape = "diel_phase") +
  # Ellipses in the background
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = morphotype), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  # Points with celestial shapes and colors
  geom_point(aes(fill = morphotype), size = 5, stroke = 1, alpha = 0.9) +  
  
  # Colors for Morphotypes
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Broad Blade" = "#800020", "Narrow Thalli" = "#BDB76B", "Filamentous" = "#C8A2C8")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Broad Blade" = "#800020", "Narrow Thalli" = "#BDB76B", "Filamentous" = "#C8A2C8")) +
  
  # Celestial Shape Mapping
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Dawn"     = 24, # Triangle Up
    "Noon"     = 21, # Circle
    "Dusk"     = 25, # Triangle Down
    "Midnight" = 8   # Star
  )) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    color = "Morphotype",
    fill = "Morphotype",
    shape = "Time of Day"
  ) +
  # Ensures the legend icons match the points
  guides(fill = "none", color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21)))


```
